anchors.fact: In 1993 Ted Breaux, a research scientist in the Louisiana petroleum industry and not in the drinks trade, heard a colleague call absinthe the green liqueur that made people crazy. He'd seen the word in New Orleans, where he grew up, without knowing exactly what it was. He read Barnaby Conrad's book on it three times, got in touch with the author, and tried distilling it himself.
anchors.meaning: *Our reading:* he fell for something he knew from a sentence and a book. Nobody asked him to; the thing itself was enough.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Ideas

anchors.fact: Then he got two old bottles of absinthe, still sealed, called them the Rosetta stones, tasted them, and said they were a lot better than what he was making.
anchors.meaning: *Our reading:* the moment he could taste the difference was also the moment he was alone with it (Wren). His motive on record is setting right an injustice; the love is ours to say, signposted.

anchors.fact: He kept going. In 2004, still unable to make it in America, he went to a distillery in France and began producing his own absinthe, a couple of thousand cases a year.
anchors.meaning: More than ten years from the sentence to the bottle. Not practice for mastery: he went back to the same thing because he loved it (Wren's line against the Old Master).

anchors.fact: *Louche* is French for cloudy, shadowy, and so disreputable. It's the word for the opal cloud that forms when water meets absinthe, as the anise oil drops out of solution. A good louche is one of the tests of a well-made absinthe.
anchors.meaning: The same word names its bad name and its beauty. What looked disreputable from outside is, from inside, the proof of care.

anchors.fact: The traditional drip: ice-cold water added slowly, about five parts to one, so the oils come out fully; drunk slowly, like wine. In the early 1800s it was sweetened with syrup in the glass; the spoon and sugar cube came later.
anchors.meaning: Ours is richer than five to one, with a cranberry syrup where the old syrup went. The cloud only comes for whoever waits for it: a thing you love opening up a little at a time.

anchors.fact: Anethole gives anise and fennel their flavour (Oxford LOUCHE; *Flavor Matrix* pdf 116); the Matrix gives fennel a surprise partner in Vaccinium, the cranberry's genus.
anchors.meaning: Tomás's build, not Breaux's. Carrying the fennel pairing over to absinthe through anethole is our inference. A love affair between two things nobody introduced.

cocktail.closingLine: Wait for the cloud. Then bring the red up into it.
cocktail.glassware: a stemmed water goblet or a large wine glass (240 ml or more)
method: Put a jug of water in the fridge with plenty of ice, so it's as cold as it gets.
Pour 15 ml of cranberry syrup into the bottom of the glass.
Pour the absinthe in slowly, down the inside of the glass, so it floats on the syrup instead of mixing into it.

Hold the jug just above the glass and let the iced water fall into the absinthe in the thinnest trickle you can, a few drops at a time (no ice in the glass). Take a minute or two. The cloud comes up from where the water lands, and the red stays underneath.
Look at it. Then stir it once, all the way to the bottom, and drink it slowly.
cocktail.name: Rosetta

preparations.text: (makes enough for a dozen drinks or more; keeps two weeks in the fridge): weigh 200 g unsweetened, 100% cranberry juice (not cranberry "cocktail") and 200 g white sugar into a jar. Close it and shake, then leave it a few minutes and shake again, until the sugar has completely dissolved. No heat.
preparations.title: Cranberry syrup

recipe.note: in the glass first, the way absinthe was sweetened before the spoon

recipe.item: Lucid absinthe (recommended), or any absinthe verte of 55% or stronger
recipe.note: Lucid is made to Ted Breaux's recipe

cocktail.tagline: The things you love become worlds you never finish exploring.

reading.epigraph: The French word for the cloud in this glass also means disreputable.
whoYouAre: There's one thing you keep going back to. A song, a recipe, a drawing you've started over so many times that nobody else can see the changes any more. People think you're repeating yourself. You're not. Every time, you notice something you missed. When someone asks why it matters so much, you explain the details, the how, the history, because "I love it" sounds like too much.

And when you finally show it to someone, you watch their face. You're not waiting for praise. You're waiting to see if they felt it too. The word that hurts you most isn't "no". It's "nice". Still, spend enough time near you and people start to care about things a little more than they planned to. You make loving something that much look like what it is: a pleasure.
yours: Ted Breaux grew up in New Orleans seeing the word absinthe, without ever knowing quite what it was. In 1993, working as a research scientist in the Louisiana oil industry, with nothing to do with bars, he heard a colleague call it the green liqueur that made people crazy. That sentence was enough. He bought a book about absinthe, read it three times, got in touch with its author, and started trying to distil it himself.

Then two old bottles of absinthe, still sealed, came into his hands. He called them his Rosetta stones. He tasted them and said plainly that they were a lot better than what he was making. He didn't stop. It was more than ten years from that first sentence to the absinthe he began making at a distillery in France in 2004. He says he did it to set right an injustice. I believe him. I also don't think anyone reads the same book three times for justice. I think you have a pair of sealed bottles of your own: the first time something got you, and you've held everything up against it since.

So this glass is mine, not his. Absinthe is made with wormwood, anise and fennel, and a book of flavour pairings gives fennel an unlikely match: cranberry. The cranberry syrup goes in first, the way absinthe was sweetened before the spoon and the sugar cube came along. The absinthe goes over it, then iced water, a few drops at a time. As the water falls, the clear green turns to a pale, shifting cloud. The French call it the louche, and the same word means shady, disreputable. Its bad name and its beauty share one word. A good cloud is one of the ways you tell it was made with care. Then one stir, and the red comes up through the white and turns it rose. The feeling doesn't spoil the careful part. It's what gives it colour.

Next time you show someone the thing you love, leave out the how. Tell them what got you, the way one sentence got him. They may never taste the difference you can. But they'll hear it in your voice, and that's the part you've been waiting for them to feel.
